statement: A signing key's own lifecycle (authorized-from/authorized-until, rotated-out, suspected-compromised, revoked) is a DISTINCT concept from the lifecycle of any credential it signed (issued/revoked/superseded), and a verifier must never conflate the two. Rotating a key out of active issuance, or marking it suspected-compromised, must NEVER erase or retroactively invalidate the historical public verification material required to validate a credential that key legitimately signed while it was authorized -- history is preserved; only future-issuance eligibility changes. A credential's signature is verifiable (or not) as a pure function of: (1) whether the signing key was registered and authorized to sign AT the specific instant the signature was created, and (2) whether the cryptographic signature itself matches -- this is fully independent of whatever the underlying subject record's CURRENT status happens to be (revoked/superseded/active), which must be composed as a separate, later layer, never merged into the same check. A key found to be REVOKED before a given signing instant makes that signature a hard, unconditional invalid (the provenance claim is false). A key found to be merely SUSPECTED COMPROMISED at a given signing instant must NEVER be auto-resolved by the verifier as either valid or invalid -- the correct, honest outcome is a distinct UNRESOLVED state, left to the credential issuer's own adjudication policy (which may draw on evidence the verifier does not have access to). A registry entry predating this lifecycle-tracking scheme entirely (no lifecycle fields recorded) must default to UNRESTRICTED (always authorized), never to a retroactively-imposed validity window that would invalidate signatures made legitimately before the scheme existed.
classification: A refinement of the Phase 3 asymmetric-signing invariant (RES-2026-09-07-DIDQUBE-PHASE-3-ASYMMETRIC-VC-SIGNING-001's 'verify signatures independently from issuance') into the temporal dimension: that resolution established WHO can verify (anyone with the public key, no shared secret); this one establishes WHEN a key's signature counts as authoritative, and what a verifier may and may not conclude when a key's own standing later changes. Distinct from the three-state UNRESOLVED pattern already used elsewhere in this codebase (types/confidentialProjection.ts's ProjectionDisposition, types/constitutionalCommerce.ts's ProjectionDisposition/FinancialServiceOutcomeStatus) -- this candidate is the SAME pattern applied to a new domain (key-authorization-at-issuance-time), not a new pattern; it is recorded as its own candidate because the underlying claim ('key lifecycle is not credential lifecycle, and the two must never be merged into one decision') is itself a reusable design rule independent of the UNRESOLVED-state mechanics it happens to reuse.

canaries.assertion: evaluateKeyAuthorizationAtTime's full boundary matrix (validFrom/validUntil inclusive bounds; revokedAt hard-invalid, never retroactive for earlier signings; compromisedAt UNRESOLVED, never auto-decided; a legacy key with no lifecycle fields authorized at any instant; revokedAt taking precedence over compromisedAt at the same instant) plus the same behavior wired end-to-end through verifyPassportCredential's Ed25519 branch.
the public verification endpoint surfaces the UNRESOLVED outcome distinctly from valid/invalid, and never collapses a compromise-window credential into a hardcoded revoked/invalid response.

occurrences.defect: Prior to this pass, the known-signing-keys registry (loadKnownSigningKeys) was a flat {keyId, publicKeyB64}[] list with no lifecycle fields at all -- a rotated-out or suspected-compromised key had no formal temporal authorization check; verification could only ever ask 'does this signature cryptographically match this key', never 'was this key allowed to sign at this moment', so a rotation or compromise event had no principled way to affect verification of credentials signed before or during it.

notes: Recorded at `candidate`, not self-promoted to `validated`/`ratified` -- per the ladder discipline, an agent must not raise a candidate above `validated`, and this pattern has exactly one recorded occurrence so far (validated requires >= 2 occurrences or demonstrated regression prevention).

The operator's own ruling (2026-09-11, quoted in full in codexes/packs/agentiq/updates/2026-09-11_didqube-phase5-1a-issuer-did-key-lifecycle.md) is the source of this candidate's substance; this record captures it as reusable engineering knowledge rather than leaving it only as a one-off implementation decision buried in code comments.

A natural second occurrence to watch for: any future subsystem in this codebase that tracks its OWN signing/attestation keys (not just the Polity Passport Bureau) should be checked against this same rule before it reinvents its own, possibly inconsistent, key-lifecycle-vs-subject-lifecycle conflation.
